reading.title: Visiting a courtroom
reading.text: On a courthouse education visit, Mira studies a model courtroom. The judge's bench is raised above the witness stand. The jury box faces the lawyers' tables. In the criminal-case example, the defense table and prosecution table are on opposite sides. Visitors sit in the gallery behind the bar, a barrier rather than a place serving drinks. Records are kept at the clerk's desk, and the bailiff's post is near the entrance. A speaker uses the podium. The guide then distinguishes the judge, jury and witness. In a separate civil-case example, the plaintiff brings a claim against the defendant. Mira learns the layout without assuming that every country's courts use the same arrangement.

reading.title: Following a mock hearing
reading.text: The adult class follows a mock hearing with an educator. The bailiff maintains order, the court reporter records the words spoken, and the clerk manages the documents. The jury foreman, also called the foreperson, speaks for the jury. An expert witness explains a specialist issue; the explanation is testimony, not proof that must automatically be accepted. An opening statement introduces one side's case, while cross-examination questions a witness. When a lawyer raises an objection, the judge may say sustained or overruled. After the closing argument, the jury's discussion is deliberation and its decision is the verdict. Sentencing is a separate stage after conviction in a criminal case. The class does not predict a real case's outcome.

reading.title: Distinguishing evidence records
reading.text: In a classroom case file, an exhibit may be a document, photograph or video offered as evidence. The instructor asks learners to separate the item from any claim about what it proves. DNA evidence comes from analysis of genetic material; a fingerprint is a pattern left by a finger. An affidavit is a written statement made under oath, whereas a deposition usually records testimony taken before trial. Forensic evidence is a broader term for information obtained through scientific examination. The class checks the descriptions and asks which source supports each claim. A photograph of a sample cannot establish its identity, reliability or legal admissibility on its own. Those questions require records, analysis and the relevant court's rules.
